interactions.summary: Jiang asks whether the class has known teachers who preach hardship now for future benefit, and one student answers that this is ordinary teacher talk about present bitterness leading to later sweetness.
A teacher in the room openly says she gives students a 'six years of hell or sixty years of hell' bargain and Jiang confirms that this approach often does produce students who reach top universities.
Jiang then opens the floor for dissenting perspectives rather than closing the issue with the success narrative alone.

claims.claim: The classroom confirms that a severe delayed-gratification narrative is standard educational rhetoric: endure six bad years now so the rest of life will be better.
Jiang does not deny that this motivational strategy can work instrumentally; he explicitly notes that many students do reach elite universities through it.
The packet frames the live debate not as a factual dispute about outcomes but as a deeper dispute about what kind of motivation education should use.

signature_moments.moment: The teacher's bargain is brutally clear: choose six years of hell now or sixty years later.
signature_moments.source_phrase: six years of hell or 60 years of hell
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It distills the whole motivational logic Jiang is testing against Virgil's rhetoric.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang grants the uncomfortable point that soul-crushing motivation can still produce measurable success.
signature_moments.source_phrase: they've gone to like really top universities
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It keeps the conversation from collapsing into an easy denunciation and forces a more serious moral argument.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The educational narrative that frames present suffering as justified by later reward and mobility.
A teacher's blunt phrase for the bargain of temporary academic suffering in exchange for later life advantage.
